Spatio-temporal copper prospectivity in the American Cordillera
predicted by positive-unlabeled machine learning
Christopher P. Alfonso, R. Dietmar Müller, Ben Mather, and Michele Anthony
EarthByte Group, School of Geosciences, University of Sydney, NSW 2006, Australia

GSA Bulletin; January/February 2025; v. 137; no. 1/2; p. 702–711
https://doi.org/10.1130/B37614.1 | Published online 29 August 2024

ABSTRACT

Porphyry copper deposits contain the majority of the world's discovered mineable reserves of
copper. While these deposits are known to form in magmatic arcs along subduction zones, the
precise contributions of different factors in the subducting and overriding plates to this process
are not well constrained, making predictive prospectivity mapping difficult.

Here we present a model trained using a semi-supervised positive-unlabeled (PU) learning
algorithm, trained using only one set of labeled data: known deposit locations. Time-dependent
and present-day mineral prospectivity maps show the past evolution and present-day state of
porphyry copper mineralization in the American Cordillera.

Feature importance and partial dependence analysis identify thick arc crust, rapid convergence,
and a sufficient supply of volatile fluids into the subduction system as the primary prerequisites
for mineralization.

METHODS — Plate Model

The plate tectonic reconstruction used throughout this work was developed from Clennett et al.
(2020), an extension of the global model of Müller et al. (2019) focused on western North
America. Further minor modifications were made using GPlates and pyGPlates.

METHODS — Training Data

Features included kinematic parameters (convergence velocity, subduction obliquity), seafloor
age (Williams et al. 2021), silicic and carbonate sediment thickness (Dutkiewicz et al. 2017,
2019), sediment pore water volume (Athy 1930), CO2 in upper oceanic crust (Müller &
Dutkiewicz 2018), overriding plate crustal thickness from paleotopography (Cao et al. 2017),
and magnetic anomaly from EMAG2v3 (Meyer et al. 2017).

427 positive observations (known porphyry copper deposits) were used. Unlabeled observations
were generated randomly at each timestep, restricted to within 6° (~667 km) of an active
subduction zone. 100 unlabeled points per 1 Myr timestep, 17,000 total.

METHODS — Classification Model

PU bagging classifier (Mordelet & Vert 2014) implemented via the pulearn package, with random
forest as the base classifier. A support vector machine (SVM) was also trained for comparison.
Prospectivity maps generated on a global 0.5°-resolution grid at 1 Myr timesteps.

RESULTS — Feature Importance (top 6, in order)

1. Mean overriding plate crustal thickness (strongest signal by a significant margin)
2. Distance to subduction zone (deposits >200 km inboard on average)
3. Orthogonal convergence rate (deposits: mean 9.02 cm/yr vs random: 5.62 cm/yr)
4. Trench velocity (deposits associated with faster trench retreat)
5. Seafloor spreading rate at origin ridge (deposits: mean 118 km/Myr vs random: 87.2 km/Myr)
6. Cumulative subducted carbonate thickness (deposits: mean 340 m vs random: 207 m)

RESULTS — Model Performance

- North America: ROC AUC ≈ 1.0 for both PU and SVM
- South America: PU ROC AUC = 0.80, SVM = 0.99 (PU underperforms)
- Full dataset: PU ROC AUC = 0.94, SVM = 0.99
